Reinforcement Learning Basics

Reinforcement learning trains an agent to make a sequence of decisions by letting it act in an environment and adjusting its behaviour to collect as much reward as possible over time. It learns from scores for outcomes, not from examples of correct actions.

AdvancedAbout 2 h 30 min (estimate)+30 XPTopic 43 of 54 in Machine Learning

1Overview

Why it matters

Supervised learning needs the right answer for every training example. Many control and decision problems have no such answers: nobody can label the correct voltage for a magnet coil ten thousand times a second, or the one video out of millions that will keep a viewer satisfied for the rest of the evening. What can be measured is the outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) is the branch of machine learning built for that situation, and it is behind game-playing agents, learned controllers for physical plants and several large recommendation and notification systems.

It is also easy to misapply. RL needs far more interaction than supervised learning needs examples, it optimises exactly the reward you wrote down and not the one you meant, and an agent that stops exploring too early settles on a poor habit without any error message. Anyone deciding whether a problem calls for RL, a simpler bandit or plain supervised learning needs the vocabulary in this lesson: states, actions, rewards, value functions, policies, and the trade-off between exploring and exploiting.

Before you start

  • Neural Network FundamentalsIntermediate
  • Probability for MLBeginner

What you will be able to do

  • Describe a decision problem as a Markov decision process by naming its states, actions, rewards, transitions and discount factor.
  • Apply the Q-learning update by hand to a small problem and reproduce the lesson's numbers in code.
  • Explain why a deep Q-network needs experience replay and a target network, and why it is limited to discrete actions.
  • State the policy-gradient idea in one sentence and explain what the critic adds in an actor-critic method.
  • Choose and justify an exploration strategy, and recognise the signs of an agent that stopped exploring too early.
  • Decide whether a problem needs full reinforcement learning, a contextual bandit or supervised learning.

Key terms

Agent and environment
The agent is the learner that chooses actions. The environment is everything else; it responds to each action with a new state and a reward.
State and observation
The state is the full description of the situation. An observation is what the agent actually gets to see, which may leave parts of the state out.
Reward and return
A reward is the number received after one step. The return is the discounted sum of all rewards from a given step to the end, and it is what the agent tries to maximise.
Policy
The agent's rule for choosing actions. It maps each state to an action, or to a probability for each action.
Markov decision process (MDP)
The formal model of the problem. It lists the states, the actions, the probabilities of moving between states, the rewards and the start states.
Discount factor (gamma)
A number between 0 and 1 that sets how much a reward one step later is worth compared with the same reward now.
Q-value (action value)
The expected return from taking a given action in a given state and behaving according to some policy afterwards.
Temporal-difference (TD) error
The gap between a value estimate and a better-informed target made from the reward just received plus the estimated value of the next state.
Exploration and exploitation
Exploitation is choosing the action currently believed to be best. Exploration is trying another action in order to learn whether it is better.
Actor and critic
In an actor-critic method the actor is the policy that picks actions, and the critic is a value function that judges how good the outcomes were.

2Explanation

Introduction

In the supervised learning you have met so far, every training example arrives with the right answer. A regression model is told the true delivery time; a classifier is told the true label. Many problems do not come with answers. Nobody can mark the correct joystick movement for each frame of a video game. What you can do is score the outcome: points won, a plasma held in shape, a reader who clicked.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning from that kind of score. A dog learning to sit is the everyday version. Nobody shows the dog the right muscle movements; it tries things, and a treat follows some of them. In RL the learner is called the agent and everything it interacts with is the environment. At each step the agent sees the current state (or an observation, a partial view of it) and picks an action. The environment answers with a new state and a reward, a single number saying how good that step was. The agent's rule for picking actions is its policy, and one run from start to finish is an episode.

The agent is not after the next reward. It wants the largest total over the whole episode, and that creates three difficulties supervised learning never meets:

  • Delayed consequences. A move that earns nothing now may be what makes a large reward possible ten steps later, so credit has to be passed backwards in time.
  • The learner produces its own data. What the agent sees next depends on what it does now. A poor policy collects poor data, and nothing in that data says what the untried actions would have earned.
  • Exploration versus exploitation. Repeating the best action found so far (exploiting) earns reward now. Trying something else (exploring) is the only way to find out whether a better action exists.

A corridor of five cells is enough to meet all three. The agent starts in cell 1. Cell 0, one step to the left, pays 1 point. Cell 4, three steps to the right, pays 10. An agent that repeats whatever has worked finds the 1-point prize first and collects it for ever. The worked example trains an agent on this corridor and shows what it takes to find the 10.

The lesson first writes the loop down formally as a Markov decision process and then covers two families of methods. Value-based methods, Q-learning and deep Q-networks, learn how good each action is and pick the best. Policy-gradient methods adjust the policy directly, and actor-critic methods combine the two. You need to know what a neural network is (neural network fundamentals), how to read an expected value (probability for ML) and what a gradient step does (gradient descent).

How it works

The problem: a Markov decision process

A Markov decision process (MDP) is the loop written down precisely. It has a set of states SSS, a set of actions AAA, a transition rule P(s′∣s,a)P(s' \mid s, a)P(s′∣s,a) giving the probability of landing in state s′s's′ after taking action aaa in state sss, a reward function and a distribution over start states. This is the five-part definition used in OpenAI's Spinning Up (opens in a new tab). "Markov" means the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on the route that led there. When the agent's input leaves out something that matters, such as the speed of a ball in a single video frame, the problem is only partially observed, and the agent needs a richer input or a memory.

A policy π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s) gives the probability of each action in each state. Write rtr_trt​ for the reward that follows the action taken at step ttt. The quantity to maximise is the expected return, the discounted sum of rewards from step ttt onwards:

Gt=rt+γrt+1+γ2rt+2+⋯=∑k=0∞γkrt+kG_t = r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 r_{t+2} + \dots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k}Gt​=rt​+γrt+1​+γ2rt+2​+⋯=k=0∑∞​γkrt+k​

The discount factor γ\gammaγ makes a reward kkk steps away worth γk\gamma^kγk of the same reward now. With γ=0\gamma = 0γ=0 the agent cares only about the next reward. Values close to 1 make it far-sighted.

Value functions and the Bellman equation

The action-value function Qπ(s,a)Q^\pi(s, a)Qπ(s,a) is the expected return from taking action aaa in state sss and following π\piπ afterwards. The optimal version Q∗(s,a)Q^*(s, a)Q∗(s,a) assumes the best possible behaviour afterwards, and it satisfies the Bellman optimality equation:

Q∗(s,a)=Es′[r+γmax⁡a′Q∗(s′,a′)]Q^*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_{s'}\Big[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \Big]Q∗(s,a)=Es′​[r+γa′max​Q∗(s′,a′)]

In words: an action is worth the reward it earns now plus the discounted value of the best action in whatever state comes next. An agent that knew Q∗Q^*Q∗ would need no planning. In every state it would take the action with the largest value. The state-value function Vπ(s)V^\pi(s)Vπ(s) is the same idea for a state alone: the expected return from sss when following π\piπ.

Q-learning: learn the values from experience

Q-learning turns the Bellman equation into an update that needs one observed transition (s,a,r,s′)(s, a, r, s')(s,a,r,s′):

Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)⏟target−Q(s,a)]Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Big[ \underbrace{r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')}_{\text{target}} - Q(s, a) \Big]Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[targetr+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)​​−Q(s,a)]

The bracket is the temporal-difference (TD) error: the gap between the current estimate and a target that is better informed, because it contains one real reward. The learning rate α\alphaα sets how far to move towards the target. When s′s's′ ends the episode, the target is rrr alone. In its simplest form QQQ is a table with one number for each state-action pair.

Two properties make this rule practical. It is model-free: it never uses PPP, only sampled transitions. It is off-policy: the target uses the best next action whatever the agent really does next, so the agent can behave in an exploratory way while learning the values of greedy behaviour. The main condition for the table to converge on Q∗Q^*Q∗, in Sutton and Barto's textbook (opens in a new tab), is that every state-action pair keeps being updated.

Exploration versus exploitation

That condition is the catch. A purely greedy agent only updates the actions it already prefers, so an early lucky reward can lock it into a poor habit. Three standard remedies:

  • ε-greedy. With probability ε\varepsilonε take a uniformly random action, otherwise the greedy one. ε\varepsilonε usually starts high and decays as the estimates improve. The DQN agent lowered it from 1.0 to 0.1 over its first million frames.
  • Optimism under uncertainty. Add a bonus to actions that have been tried rarely. The UCB rule picks the action that maximises Q(a)+cln⁡t/N(a)Q(a) + c\sqrt{\ln t / N(a)}Q(a)+clnt/N(a)​, where N(a)N(a)N(a) counts how often aaa has been tried, so uncertainty itself attracts trials. LinUCB (opens in a new tab) applies the same idea to news recommendation with a linear model.
  • Sampling from a stochastic policy. Choose actions with probabilities given by a softmax of their scores. Policy-gradient methods explore this way by construction.

How much exploration you can afford depends on what a bad action costs. Random moves in a game emulator are free. Random recommendations to real users are not.

The trade-off already exists in the simplest setting, the bandit: one decision per episode, an immediate reward and no next state. When each decision also comes with features describing the situation it is a contextual bandit. Bandits are RL without the delayed consequences.

Deep Q-networks: replace the table with a network

A table cannot hold one row for every possible screen image. A deep Q-network (DQN) is a neural network with weights θ\thetaθ that takes the state as input and outputs one Q-value per action. It is trained by gradient descent on the squared TD error:

L(θ)=E(s,a,r,s′)∼D[(r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′;θ−)−Q(s,a;θ))2]L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, r, s') \sim D}\Big[\big(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-) - Q(s, a; \theta)\big)^2\Big]L(θ)=E(s,a,r,s′)∼D​[(r+γa′max​Q(s′,a′;θ−)−Q(s,a;θ))2]

Combining a target that depends on the network's own output with a nonlinear network can oscillate or diverge. The DQN paper (opens in a new tab) made it work with two additions:

  • Experience replay. Transitions go into a buffer DDD, and each update uses a random minibatch drawn from it. Consecutive steps are strongly correlated; random sampling breaks that up, and each transition is reused in many updates.
  • A target network. The target is computed with an older copy of the weights, θ−\theta^-θ−, which is refreshed only every CCC updates. Without it, each update would shift the target it is chasing.

Because acting means taking the largest of the network's outputs, DQN needs a small, discrete set of actions. The Stable-Baselines3 DQN implementation (opens in a new tab) accepts discrete action spaces only.

Policy gradients: adjust the policy directly

The second family skips the value table. It parameterises the policy itself, πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a \mid s)πθ​(a∣s), usually as a network whose outputs pass through a softmax, and moves θ\thetaθ uphill on the expected return J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ). The gradient can be estimated from sampled episodes. In the form implementations use, with GtG_tGt​ the return that followed step ttt (Spinning Up, part 3 (opens in a new tab)):

∇θJ(θ)=Eπθ[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) Gt]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\Big[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\, G_t\Big]∇θ​J(θ)=Eπθ​​[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​]

The REINFORCE algorithm applies this literally. Play episodes with the current policy, then make each action that was taken more likely in proportion to the return that followed it. Nothing here requires a maximum over actions, so the method works for continuous actions and for action sets with millions of members. It has two costs. It is on-policy: the expectation is over episodes from the current policy, so data gathered by an older policy cannot simply be reused. And the estimate is noisy, because GtG_tGt​ adds up many random rewards.

Actor-critic: a learned baseline

Subtracting a baseline that depends only on the state leaves the expected gradient unchanged and can reduce its variance a great deal. The natural baseline is the state value, which turns the weight on each action into an advantage: how much better things went than expected from that state.

∇θJ(θ)≈∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) (Gt−Vϕ(st))\nabla_\theta J(\theta) \approx \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\,\big(G_t - V_\phi(s_t)\big)∇θ​J(θ)≈t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−Vϕ​(st​))

An actor-critic method learns both parts together. The actor is the policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​. The critic is a value network VϕV_\phiVϕ​, trained by regression towards observed returns or towards the one-step target r+γVϕ(s′)r + \gamma V_\phi(s')r+γVϕ​(s′). In the second case the TD error r+γVϕ(s′)−Vϕ(s)r + \gamma V_\phi(s') - V_\phi(s)r+γVϕ​(s′)−Vϕ​(s) serves as the advantage estimate, as the Hugging Face course's A2C unit (opens in a new tab) explains. A2C, A3C and PPO follow this pattern. DDPG and SAC pair an actor with a Q-function critic, which lets them learn off-policy with continuous actions (Spinning Up, part 2 (opens in a new tab)). The critic is needed only for training. When decisions are made, the actor runs alone.

Worked example: Q-learning in a five-cell corridor with a small prize nearby and a large one far away

A corridor has five cells numbered 0 to 4. The agent starts in cell 1 and moves one cell left or right per step. Stepping into cell 0 pays 1 and ends the episode. Stepping into cell 4 pays 10 and ends the episode. Every other step pays 0. The discount factor is γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 and the learning rate is α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5.

Step 2: four episodes by hand

Start with every Q-value at 0 and apply Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+0.5 [target−Q(s,a)]Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + 0.5\,[\text{target} - Q(s,a)]Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+0.5[target−Q(s,a)] after each move.

EpisodeMovesValues after the episode
AleftQ(1, left) = 0 + 0.5 × (1 − 0) = 0.5
Bright, right, rightQ(1, right) = 0, Q(2, right) = 0, Q(3, right) = 0 + 0.5 × (10 − 0) = 5
Cright, right, rightQ(1, right) = 0, Q(2, right) = 0.5 × (0.9 × 5) = 2.25, Q(3, right) = 5 + 0.5 × (10 − 5) = 7.5
Dright, right, rightQ(1, right) = 0.5 × (0.9 × 2.25) = 1.0125, Q(2, right) = 2.25 + 0.5 × (6.75 − 2.25) = 4.5, Q(3, right) = 8.75

News of the 10 travels backwards one cell per episode: it reaches cell 3 in episode B, cell 2 in C and the start cell in D. Only after D does Q(1, right) = 1.0125 exceed Q(1, left) = 0.5. A greedy agent would never have played episodes B to D, because after episode A left already looked better than right (0.5 against 0).

Step 3: run it with three exploration settings

The code uses only the Python standard library.

python
import random

GAMMA, ALPHA = 0.9, 0.5
LEFT, RIGHT = 0, 1

def step(state, action):
    """Cells 0..4. Reaching cell 0 pays 1 and reaching cell 4 pays 10; both end the episode."""
    nxt = state - 1 if action == LEFT else state + 1
    return nxt, {0: 1.0, 4: 10.0}.get(nxt, 0.0), nxt in (0, 4)

def choose(q, state, epsilon, rng):
    left, right = q[state]
    if rng.random() < epsilon or left == right:      # explore, or break a tie at random
        return LEFT if rng.random() < 0.5 else RIGHT
    return LEFT if left > right else RIGHT           # exploit

def train(epsilon_for, episodes=400, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    q = {s: [0.0, 0.0] for s in range(5)}            # q[state] = [Q(left), Q(right)]
    prizes = []
    for episode in range(episodes):
        state, done = 1, False
        while not done:
            action = choose(q, state, epsilon_for(episode), rng)
            nxt, reward, done = step(state, action)
            target = reward if done else reward + GAMMA * max(q[nxt])
            q[state][action] += ALPHA * (target - q[state][action])
            state = nxt
        prizes.append(reward)                        # 1 or 10
    return q, prizes

schedules = {
    "always greedy (epsilon 0)": lambda episode: 0.0,
    "constant epsilon 0.1": lambda episode: 0.1,
    "epsilon 1.0 falling to 0.05 over 100 episodes": lambda episode: max(0.05, 1.0 - 0.95 * episode / 100),
}
for name, epsilon_for in schedules.items():
    q, prizes = train(epsilon_for)
    table = "   ".join(f"cell {s}: {q[s][0]:.2f} | {q[s][1]:.2f}" for s in (1, 2, 3))
    print(f"{name}\n  mean prize, last 100 episodes: {sum(prizes[-100:]) / 100:.2f}\n  Q(left) | Q(right)   {table}")

constant epsilon 0.1

Step 4: read the result

  • The greedy agent reached cell 0 in its first episode, learned Q(1, left) and never tried anything else.
  • Constant ε = 0.1 did not rescue this run. Q(2, left) = 0.90 shows why. On the rare occasions the agent stepped right into cell 2, the only value it knew pointed back at the small prize (0.9 × 1), so its greedy move from cell 2 was left again. To reach cell 4 it must explore at cell 1, explore again at cell 2 and then also pick right at cell 3.
  • The decaying schedule acts almost at random at first, finds both prizes, and then exploits. Its table equals Q∗Q^*Q∗ from Step 1 to two decimals. The mean prize is 9.91 and not 10 because with ε = 0.05 about one episode in 40 still begins with a random step left.

One seed proves little, so the plot repeats the experiment for seeds 0 to 1,999.

After 400 episodes the learned greedy policy was the optimal one in 4% of runs with ε = 0, 47% with ε = 0.1, 94% with ε = 0.3 and 1,999 of 2,000 runs with the decaying schedule. Constant ε = 0.3 finds the large prize but keeps giving reward away on random steps. The schedule explores when knowledge is poor and stops paying for it once knowledge is good.

Edge cases and limitations

A time limit is not a terminal state
Gymnasium's step function returns two separate flags: terminated, when the task itself ended, and truncated, when a step limit cut the episode short. After a truncation the last state was not really final, so the Q-learning target should still include the discounted value of the next state. Dropping it teaches the agent that states reached late in an episode are worthless. Set the bootstrap term to zero only when terminated is true.
The observation leaves out part of the state
A single Atari frame does not show which way the ball is moving, so one frame is not a Markov state. The DQN agent took the four most recent preprocessed frames as its input for this reason. If your observation omits something that changes the future, such as a velocity or the time since the last notification, add recent history to the input or use a recurrent network. Otherwise one observation stands for several different situations and the learned values average over them.
Random transitions need a small learning rate
In Gymnasium's FrozenLake with is_slippery=True the agent moves in the intended direction one time in three and sideways otherwise. Each Q-learning target is then one noisy sample, and a large learning rate keeps overwriting the estimate with whatever happened last. In the first exercise of this lesson a learning rate of 0.5 gives policies whose success rate swings between 15% and 73% across five seeds, while 0.05 gives 72% every time, close to the 73% of the best possible policy.
The reward can be maximised in a way you did not intend
The agent optimises the number you defined and nothing else. The DQN authors clipped all rewards to −1, 0 or +1 so that one learning rate would work across games, and they note that the agent can then no longer tell a large reward from a small one. Facebook's notification policy includes an explicit penalty for each notification sent in order to control volume. Before training, work out what the highest-scoring behaviour would be for an agent that ignores your intent.
Rare rewards defeat random exploration
ε-greedy finds a reward only if random actions happen to reach it. In the five-cell corridor that takes several unlikely steps in a row, and with a constant ε of 0.1 fewer than half of the runs had learned to prefer the large prize after 400 episodes. The DQN paper reports that games needing long chains of deliberate actions, such as Montezuma's Revenge, remained a major challenge. A high starting ε, a more informative (shaped) reward or an uncertainty bonus are the usual responses.
The same settings succeed with one random seed and fail with another
In the worked example, constant ε = 0.1 is stuck on the small prize with seed 0 and learns the optimal table with seed 1. The Stable-Baselines3 documentation gives the same warning for deep RL: results may vary from one run to the next when only the seed changes. Run several seeds, report the spread, and measure performance in a separate evaluation environment with exploration switched off.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • Decisions come in a sequence and each action changes the situations the agent will face later, so the best choice now depends on what it sets up.
  • You can measure how well things went but cannot label the correct action for each situation.
  • You have a simulator, an emulator or another cheap and safe place where the agent can make millions of mistakes.
  • You run a live system in which each decision can be randomised a little and its probability logged, so that a policy can be learned and evaluated from the logs.

Think twice when

  • You have examples of the correct output. Supervised learning is simpler, more stable and needs far less data.
  • Each decision is independent of the next and its payoff is visible at once. A contextual bandit or an A/B test answers that without value functions or discounting.
  • Exploring is dangerous or expensive and you have neither a trustworthy simulator nor logged data with action probabilities.
  • You cannot express the goal as a number that is measured within a reasonable time after the action.

A simpler alternative. Train a supervised model that predicts the immediate outcome of each action, for example the click probability of each article, and choose the action with the best prediction, with a little ε-greedy randomisation so that the logs stay informative. That is a contextual bandit. It stops being enough when today's action changes tomorrow's options or responses, as when frequent notifications wear out a person's attention. At that point the delayed effect has to be modelled with returns and value functions.

Key takeaways

  • Reinforcement learning learns from rewards for outcomes instead of labelled correct actions, and the agent's own behaviour decides which data it gets to learn from.
  • A Markov decision process describes the problem with states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor, and the goal is the largest expected discounted return, not the largest next reward.
  • Q-learning moves each action value towards the reward received plus the discounted value of the best next action, and a deep Q-network does the same with a neural network stabilised by experience replay and a target network.
  • Policy-gradient methods raise the probability of actions in proportion to the return that followed them, and an actor-critic adds a learned value function so that only better-than-expected outcomes are reinforced.
  • An agent that never explores can lock onto the first reward it finds, so exploration must be deliberate, usually high at the start and lower later, and its cost limits what can be done on live systems.
  • RL needs large amounts of safe interaction and a carefully designed reward, so when decisions are independent or labelled answers exist, a bandit or supervised learning is the better tool.

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Reinforcement Learning Basics. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. DeepMind DQN: one agent design that learned 49 Atari games from pixels and score
  2. Facebook Horizon: a DQN trained on logged decisions chooses which notifications to send
  3. YouTube: a REINFORCE policy over millions of videos, corrected for learning from logs
  4. DeepMind and EPFL: an actor-critic controller for tokamak plasma, trained in a simulator
  5. Microsoft Decision Service on MSN: ε-greedy exploration for the news homepage

Example 1 of 5

DeepMind DQN: one agent design that learned 49 Atari games from pixels and score

Google DeepMindDocumented in a paper

DeepMind's 2015 Nature paper "Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning", read here from the PDF that DeepMind hosts, describes an agent called the deep Q-network (DQN) that learns to play Atari 2600 games inside an emulator. A 2013 arXiv paper by the same group reports the first version on seven games, and a 2016 DeepMind blog post by David Silver summarises the work. [13][15][14]

The problem

Learn to act well directly from high-dimensional input, a 210 × 160 colour video stream at 60 Hz, when the only feedback is the game score. A Q-table is impossible because there are far too many distinct screens, and Q-learning combined with a neural network had a record of unstable training. The authors also wanted one method that works across many different games without game-specific tuning.

Where this topic fits

Q-learning is the learning rule and a convolutional network replaces the table. The network's input is a stack of the last four preprocessed frames and it has one output per joystick action, so a single forward pass gives every Q-value needed for the greedy choice. ε-greedy exploration in the emulator generates the data. Experience replay and a separate target network sit between acting and learning to keep training stable.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Preprocess each frame to an 84 × 84 luminance image and stack the four most recent frames as the state, so that motion is visible to the network.
  2. Choose the action ε-greedily from the network's outputs and repeat it for four frames. ε falls linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first million frames and then stays at 0.1.
  3. Clip the reward to −1, 0 or +1 and store the transition (state, action, reward, next state) in a replay memory that holds the most recent million frames.
  4. Draw a random minibatch of 32 stored transitions and compute each target as the reward plus the discounted largest Q-value of the next state according to the target network.
  5. Take a gradient step that moves the online network's Q-value for the stored action towards the target.
  6. After every C updates copy the online network's weights into the target network, and continue for 50 million frames per game.

Why this approach fits

The emulator supplies unlimited interaction at no cost, so the agent can afford 50 million frames and an ε that starts at fully random behaviour. The action set is small and discrete (the paper reports between 4 and 18 valid actions per game), which is what the argmax in Q-learning needs. Q-learning is off-policy, so transitions gathered by old, more random versions of the agent are still valid training data. That property is what makes a replay memory possible at all, and replay in turn lets each frame be used in many updates.

Limitation or tradeoff

The sample cost is very high: the paper equates 50 million frames to about 38 days of game experience for each game. Reward clipping hides the difference between a small and a large score. Undirected ε-greedy exploration rarely completes the long sequences of deliberate actions that some games demand, and the authors name Montezuma's Revenge as an example that remains a major challenge. The recipe also assumes a fast simulator, which most real problems do not have.

What the sources document

  • The agent received only the pixels and the game score as inputs. A different network was trained on each of 49 Atari 2600 games with the same algorithm, architecture and hyperparameters, and it achieved more than 75% of a professional human games tester's score on more than half of the games (29 games). [13]
  • The behaviour policy during training was ε-greedy with ε annealed linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first million frames and fixed at 0.1 thereafter. Training ran for 50 million frames, described as around 38 days of game experience, with a replay memory of the 1 million most recent frames and minibatches of size 32. [13]
  • The paper modifies online Q-learning in two ways: experience replay, and a separate target network that is cloned from the Q-network every C updates. It explains that generating targets from an older set of parameters adds a delay that makes divergence or oscillations much more unlikely. [13]
  • During training all positive rewards were clipped at 1 and all negative rewards at −1, and the authors note that the agent then cannot differentiate between rewards of different magnitude. They state that games demanding more temporally extended planning strategies, for example Montezuma's Revenge, remain a major challenge. [13]
  • The 2013 paper lists as advantages of experience replay that each step of experience can be used in many weight updates and that randomising the samples breaks the correlations between consecutive samples. DeepMind's 2016 post describes the same mechanism as storing all of the agent's experiences and randomly sampling and replaying them to provide diverse and decorrelated training data, and says separate DQN agents were trained for 50 different Atari games. [15][14]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

Facebook Horizon: a DQN trained on logged decisions chooses which notifications to send

Facebook (Meta)Documented in a paper

Horizon is the applied reinforcement learning platform that Facebook open-sourced in 2018. The platform's paper and the accompanying Facebook Engineering post describe how it was used to decide whether to send or drop push notification candidates. [16][17]

The problem

Facebook previously scored notifications with supervised models that predicted click-through rate and the likelihood of a meaningful interaction. The paper says this did not capture the long-term or incremental value of sending a notification. There is also no simulator of people to train against: the paper describes applied problems where datasets are large, the feedback loop is slow, and experiments must be done with care because they do not run in a simulator.

Where this topic fits

The decision is modelled as an MDP over the sequence of notification candidates for one person. A discrete-action DQN is trained offline on logged transitions produced by the existing system. Before a new policy is deployed, counterfactual policy evaluation estimates how it would have performed on the logged data. After deployment the model is retrained on the data its own decisions generate.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Define the MDP: the state is a set of features about the person and the notification candidate, the actions are send and drop, and the reward combines interactions and activity with a penalty for sending.
  2. Log every decision of the running system with its state features, the action taken, the probability with which that action was taken, the outcome metrics and the possible actions.
  3. Join each logged row with the next row of the same person to form transitions, and compute the reward as a weighted sum of the logged metrics.
  4. Train the DQN on batches of these transitions. No environment is stepped during training; the logged next state plays the role of the environment's answer.
  5. Estimate the new policy's value from the logs with counterfactual policy evaluation, using the logged action probabilities, before exposing people to it.
  6. Serve the policy: send when the sigmoid of Q(send) minus Q(drop) reaches a threshold. Retrain daily on data from people exposed to the model.

Why this approach fits

Sending a notification now changes how the same person responds to the next one, so the decisions are linked through time and a model of the immediate click misses part of the effect. A value function over the sequence can represent that. DQN is off-policy, which is the property that lets it learn from logs written by the previous system instead of from its own trial and error, and with only two actions the maximum over actions is trivial.

Limitation or tradeoff

Learning from logs can only judge actions that the logging system took at least sometimes in similar states, and counterfactual estimates are estimates, not measurements. The behaviour of the policy is set by the reward weights, including the size of the sending penalty, which are chosen by people. The sources report the outcome in words, as a significant improvement, without publishing figures.

What the sources document

  • Horizon is designed for applied problems where datasets are large (millions to billions of observations), the feedback loop is slow compared with a simulator, and experiments must be done with care because they do not run in a simulator. [16]
  • For push notifications the MDP is based on a sequence of notification candidates for a particular person. The actions are sending and dropping the notification, the state describes features of the person and the candidate, and there are rewards for interactions and activity on Facebook with a penalty for sending to control the volume of notifications. [16]
  • Facebook had historically used supervised learning models that predict click-through rate and the likelihood of meaningful interactions, which did not capture the long-term or incremental value of sending notifications. The paper reports a significant improvement in activity and meaningful interactions after deploying an RL-based policy for certain types of notifications. [16]
  • The logged training table has an action probability column, the probability that the current system took the logged action, which is used in counterfactual policy evaluation. The model was incrementally retrained daily on data from people exposed to the model. [16]
  • The engineering post says a discrete-action DQN model was trained for sending push notifications, that the model lets a notification through only when its value to the person is higher than the penalty, and that relevance improved without an increase in the total number of notifications. [17]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

YouTube: a REINFORCE policy over millions of videos, corrected for learning from logs

Google (YouTube)Documented in a paper

The paper "Top-K Off-Policy Correction for a REINFORCE Recommender System" by Google researchers describes a production candidate generator at YouTube that is trained with the policy-gradient algorithm REINFORCE and evaluated in live A/B experiments. [18]

The problem

The recommender has to pick from many millions of items for a very large number of users, so a method that needs a maximum over all action values is impractical. The learner cannot interact with users freely either: it only receives logged feedback on items that earlier versions of the recommender chose to show, and that data is biased towards what those versions preferred. Finally, the system shows several items at once, not one.

Where this topic fits

The policy is a softmax over items computed from a recurrent network's summary of the user's recent activity. REINFORCE weights the log-probability of each logged action by the discounted future reward that followed. Because the logged actions came from other policies, each term is multiplied by an importance weight and by a further factor that accounts for recommending K items. At serving time the policy is sampled, which is the system's exploration mechanism.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Cast recommendation as an MDP: the state is a learned vector describing the user, an action is an item to recommend, and the reward reflects the user's activity. A recommended video that is not clicked earns zero.
  2. Parameterise the policy as a softmax over items on top of a recurrent network, and train it with a sampled softmax because the full sum over millions of items is too expensive.
  3. For each logged action, compute the discounted future reward that followed it and use it as the weight in the REINFORCE gradient.
  4. Multiply each term by the ratio of the new policy's probability to the logging policy's probability for that action. The logging probability is itself estimated by a second softmax head, and the ratio is capped to limit variance.
  5. Multiply by the top-K factor, which boosts items the policy currently gives little probability and fades out once an item is likely to appear among the K shown.
  6. Serve by looking up the most probable items with nearest-neighbour search, returning the top few and sampling the rest from the softmax, so that less-shown items still receive feedback.

Why this approach fits

A policy gradient needs only the probability of the action that was actually taken, so it scales to an action set of millions where an argmax over Q-values does not. The policy is stochastic by design, which gives a controlled form of exploration: sampling from the model's own distribution instead of showing uniformly random videos. And the objective is the reward that follows over hours, not the immediate click.

Limitation or tradeoff

REINFORCE is an on-policy method being fed off-policy data, so correctness rests on importance weights that raise variance and on an estimated logging policy. The paper's first-order approximation is knowingly biased, and the weight cap is a sensitive setting: raising it from e³ to e⁵ lowered ViewTime by 0.52% in a live test. The measured gains are fractions of a percent, which only a system with very large traffic can detect.

What the sources document

  • The abstract describes a production top-K recommender at YouTube built with a policy-gradient-based algorithm, REINFORCE, and lists as contributions scaling REINFORCE to an action space on the order of millions and applying off-policy correction to biases in logged feedback collected from multiple behaviour policies. [18]
  • The learner does not have real-time interactive control of the recommender; it receives logged feedback of actions chosen by historical policies. The paper's first-order approximation of the importance weight yields a slightly biased estimator of the policy gradient with lower variance. [18]
  • In a live experiment with K = 16 and a weight cap of e³, the top-K off-policy correction increased ViewTime by 0.85% compared with the standard off-policy correction, while the number of videos viewed decreased slightly, by 0.16%. [18]
  • The paper states that brute-force exploration such as ε-greedy is not viable in a production system like YouTube and uses Boltzmann exploration, sampling from the softmax policy. Serving a stochastic policy trained with exploratory data to 5% of users gave a statistically significant 0.07% increase in ViewTime. [18]
  • Videos that are recommended but not clicked receive zero reward, the long-term reward is aggregated over a time horizon of 4 to 10 hours, and the model is trained continuously on new events with a lag under 24 hours. [18]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

DeepMind and EPFL: an actor-critic controller for tokamak plasma, trained in a simulator

Google DeepMind and the EPFL Swiss Plasma CenterDocumented in a paper

The open-access Nature paper "Magnetic control of tokamak plasmas through deep reinforcement learning" (2022), read here in the full text served by Europe PMC, and DeepMind's blog post about it describe a learned controller that was run on TCV, the variable-configuration tokamak in Lausanne. [19][20]

The problem

A tokamak holds a plasma in place with magnetic fields, and the fields must be adjusted continuously through the voltages on 19 control coils. The paper describes the conventional solution as a set of independent single-input single-output PID controllers that must be designed not to interfere with one another, and presents the learned approach as a notable reduction in the design effort needed for a new plasma configuration. Learning by trial and error on the machine is not possible: the blog notes that TCV sustains a plasma for at most three seconds and then needs 15 minutes to cool down.

Where this topic fits

Reinforcement learning replaces the controller design step. Engineers state what the plasma should do, those objectives are turned into a reward, and an actor-critic algorithm (MPO) learns a control policy entirely inside a physics simulator. Only the actor, a small network, is taken to the real machine, where it maps sensor readings to coil voltage commands at 10 kHz.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Specify objectives such as plasma current, position and shape targets. Each is converted into a quality measure between 0 and 1 and the measures are combined into one scalar reward per time step.
  2. Add termination conditions that stop a simulated run and give a large negative reward when operating limits are violated, so the policy learns to stay away from those regions.
  3. Run many copies of the simulator in parallel, each controlled by the current policy, and collect the interactions in a buffer.
  4. Train the critic on that data to predict the discounted future reward of actions, and update the actor using the critic's predictions.
  5. Keep the actor small enough to be evaluated within 50 microseconds, while giving the critic a larger recurrent network, since the critic never leaves the training cluster.
  6. Compile the trained actor and run it on TCV without further tuning of its weights.

Why this approach fits

The action is a vector of 19 continuous voltages, which rules out a Q-network with one output per action and points to a policy network. A critic makes learning that policy far less noisy, and the split between actor and critic matches the engineering constraint exactly: only the part that must run in real time has to be small. The simulator supplies the volume of experience that a machine with three-second experiments never could.

Limitation or tradeoff

Everything depends on the simulator being right where the policy operates. The authors say there are known regions where the dynamics are poorly represented, and that the controllers are not guaranteed to avoid plasma disruptions. Training is expensive as well: one to three days with 5,000 simulator instances running in parallel.

What the sources document

  • The paper uses maximum a posteriori policy optimisation (MPO), which it describes as an actor-critic algorithm: the critic learns the discounted expected future reward for various actions, and the actor uses the critic's predictions to set the control policy. [19]
  • The actor's representation of the control policy is restricted because it must run on TCV with real-time guarantees, whereas the critic is unrestricted because it is only used during training. The critic network has 718,337 parameters and uses a recurrent LSTM; the policy network has 266,280 parameters. [19]
  • The control policy consumes TCV's magnetic and current sensors at a 10 kHz control rate, using 34 wire loops that measure magnetic flux, 38 probes that measure the local magnetic field and 19 measurements of the current in the active control coils, and must be evaluated within 50 microseconds. [19]
  • Training used 5,000 actors in parallel, generally taking one to three days, and experiments were executed without further tuning of the policy network's weights, which the paper calls zero-shot transfer from simulation to hardware. The authors state that the controllers are not guaranteed to avoid plasma disruptions. [19]
  • DeepMind's post says TCV has 19 magnetic coils whose voltage must be adjusted thousands of times per second, and that the machine can sustain the plasma in a single experiment for up to three seconds, after which it needs 15 minutes to cool down. [20]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

Microsoft Decision Service on MSN: ε-greedy exploration for the news homepage

MicrosoftDocumented in a paper

The paper "Making Contextual Decisions with Low Technical Debt" by Microsoft researchers describes the Decision Service, a system for contextual bandit learning, and its production deployment for ordering news articles on the MSN homepage. [21]

The problem

When a user requests the homepage, MSN must decide how to order the articles. Feedback is partial: a click is observed only for what was shown. The paper points out that such settings are prone to bias because the system's own decisions determine the data it is later trained on, and that a biased dataset, however large, does not enable good learning. The editors' ordering was the default policy and had beaten earlier attempts to use machine learning.

Where this topic fits

This is the exploration-exploitation trade-off in its purest form: a contextual bandit, which is reinforcement learning with a single step per episode and no state transition. Exploration is built into the decision itself through an ε-greedy policy on live traffic. The probability of each choice is logged with it, which makes the data usable both for training and for evaluating other policies offline.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. A request arrives with its context: for logged-in users, demographics and the topics of stories they clicked before. The actions are the articles currently selected by the editors, typically tens of them.
  2. Explore: with probability ε choose an article uniformly at random, otherwise follow the current learned policy. Record the context, the action and the probability with which it was chosen.
  3. Log: join that record with the reward, a click or no click, observed within a fixed window after the decision.
  4. Learn: update the policy online from this exploration data.
  5. Deploy: publish the new model to the component that makes decisions, and repeat the loop every few minutes because news goes stale quickly.
  6. Evaluate any candidate policy offline by inverse propensity scoring: add up the rewards of the logged decisions that the candidate agrees with, each divided by its logged probability, and divide by the total number of logged decisions.

Why this approach fits

Each homepage request is a separate decision whose payoff, a click, arrives within minutes, so the one-step bandit model is adequate and the machinery of value functions is unnecessary. News is non-stationary: articles appear and age within hours, so exploration cannot be switched off after an initial phase. Logging the probability of every decision turns live traffic into a dataset on which any other policy can be scored without another live experiment.

Limitation or tradeoff

An ε of 33% means roughly a third of decisions ignore the learned policy. That is a real cost in clicks, easier to accept here because every candidate article was already selected by editors. A bandit optimises the immediate click and cannot see longer-term effects; the paper reports checking that click-through was aligned with session metrics in this case. Inverse propensity estimates become noisy when the logged probabilities are small or the candidate policy rarely agrees with the log.

What the sources document

  • On MSN the front-end servers must decide how to order the articles on the homepage. The action choices are the current set of news articles selected and ranked by editors, typically tens of articles, and the reward signal is clicks. The deployment is the production default, serving tens of millions of users who issue thousands of requests per second. [21]
  • The default exploration policy EpsilonGreedy is used with ε = 33%. The experimental unit is set to 10 minutes and a new model is deployed to the client library every 5 minutes. [21]
  • In A/B tests against the editorial ordering, experiments on the Slate segment of the page showed a CTR improvement of more than 25% over a two-week period and the Panel segment showed a 5.3% improvement. MSN made the service the default in production for all logged-in users in early 2016. [21]
  • The paper argues that it is not possible to learn that a sports article generates more clicks than a politics article for a given demographic without showing both types at least some of the time, so there is a need to explore to acquire the right data. [21]
  • With inverse propensity scoring, any policy can be evaluated regardless of how the data was collected. The estimator sums the reward divided by the logged probability over the datapoints where the policy's action matches the logged action, and divides by the number of datapoints. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Switching exploration off, or letting ε decay to zero, before the agent has seen the better outcomes.

    Why it causes problems
    A greedy agent only updates the actions it already prefers, so the values of everything else stay at their initial guesses and the policy settles, with full confidence, on the first reward it found. In the corridor, 96% of the runs with ε = 0 end up collecting the 1-point prize for ever.
    How to recognise it
    The return flattens early at a level below what you know is achievable, the Q-values of rarely chosen actions are still at their initial value, and different seeds settle at different levels.
    How to fix it
    Start ε near 1 and lower it to a small floor over a substantial part of training, and count how often each action was tried in the important states. On a live bandit-style system keep a permanent small ε and log the probability of each decision.

  2. Breaking ties between equal Q-values by always taking the first action.

    Why it causes problems
    With a zero-initialised table every state is a tie at the start, and an argmax that returns the first index sends the agent in the same direction every time. In the frozen-lake exercise with a constant ε of 0.1 the agent then spends 2,000 episodes pushing against the left wall and never reaches the goal.
    How to recognise it
    Early episodes repeat one action, the visited states cluster around the start, and the Q-table is still all zeros after many episodes.
    How to fix it
    Choose uniformly at random among the actions that share the maximum, or begin with ε = 1 so that early behaviour is random whatever the tie rule is.

  3. Treating an episode cut off by a time limit as if it had reached a terminal state.

    Why it causes problems
    The target then leaves out the value of the next state, so every state the agent tends to be in when the clock runs out is taught to be worth less than it is. The error spreads backwards through the value estimates and biases the policy away from long, successful episodes.
    How to recognise it
    The code computes done = terminated or truncated and uses done to zero the bootstrap term. Value estimates dip for states that occur late in episodes.
    How to fix it
    Use terminated alone when building the target, and use terminated or truncated only to decide when to reset the environment.

  4. Judging an agent by the rewards it collected during training, from a single run.

    Why it causes problems
    Training episodes contain exploratory actions, so they understate what the learned policy can do, and one seed can be lucky or unlucky. Decisions about algorithms and hyperparameters made on that basis often do not reproduce.
    How to recognise it
    The report shows one learning curve and no separate evaluation, and rerunning with a different seed changes the conclusion.
    How to fix it
    At regular intervals evaluate the policy without exploration on a separate copy of the environment for a fixed number of episodes; the Stable-Baselines3 guide suggests 5 to 20. Repeat the whole experiment with several seeds and report the mean and the spread.

  5. Feeding old logged data to a policy-gradient update as if the current policy had produced it.

    Why it causes problems
    The REINFORCE gradient is an average over episodes from the current policy. Data from another policy over-represents that policy's favourite actions, so the update mostly learns to copy it. The YouTube paper calls the result a "rich get richer" effect.
    How to recognise it
    A replay buffer or a historical log feeds an on-policy algorithm with no importance weights, and the new policy's choices closely mirror those of the system that produced the log.
    How to fix it
    Collect fresh data for each update, or switch to an off-policy method from the Q-learning family, or weight each term by the ratio of the new policy's probability to the logging policy's probability and cap that ratio.

5Practice

Exercise 1

Q-learning on the frozen lake, first without and then with slippery ice

CodingIntermediateAbout 1 h (estimate)

Gymnasium's FrozenLake (opens in a new tab) environment is a 4 × 4 grid. The agent starts at S and must reach G. Stepping into a hole H ends the episode with no reward. Reaching G pays 1 and every other step pays 0. This exercise re-implements the environment in a few lines so that it runs with the Python standard library alone. The map, the numbering of states and actions and the slippery rule are the documented ones.

text
S F F F      states are numbered row * 4 + column, so S is 0 and G is 15
F H F H      actions: 0 = left, 1 = down, 2 = right, 3 = up
F F F H      a move into the edge of the grid leaves the agent where it is
H F F G
python
import random

MAP = ["SFFF", "FHFH", "FFFH", "HFFG"]
MOVES = [(0, -1), (1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0)]          # 0 left, 1 down, 2 right, 3 up

def step(state, action, rng, slippery):
    if slippery:                                     # intended move or a perpendicular one, 1/3 each
        action = (action + rng.choice((-1, 0, 1))) % 4
    row, col = divmod(state, 4)
    d_row, d_col = MOVES[action]
    row, col = min(3, max(0, row + d_row)), min(3, max(0, col + d_col))
    cell = MAP[row][col]
    return row * 4 + col, float(cell == "G"), cell in "HG"   # next state, reward, terminated

Use γ=0.95\gamma = 0.95γ=0.95 and a limit of 100 steps per episode.

  1. Write tabular Q-learning with a table of zeros, random tie-breaking among the best actions, and ε falling linearly from 1.0 to 0.05 over the first half of training. Train for 2,000 episodes with α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 on the non-slippery lake. Report the largest Q-value in the start state and the fraction of 2,000 greedy test episodes that reach G.
  2. Before you run it, predict that largest Q-value by hand.
  3. Change two things: break ties by always taking the first best action, and hold ε constant at 0.1. Train again and explain what you see.
  4. Return to the settings of part 1, switch slippery on and train for 20,000 episodes, once with α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 and once with α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05. Compare the success rates and explain the difference.

Requirements

  • The learning code must use only what step returns; it must not read MAP.
  • Set the bootstrap term to zero only when terminated is true. Reaching the 100-step limit must not zero it.
  • Evaluate with a purely greedy policy on separate test episodes that use a different random seed.
  • Keep gamma at 0.95 throughout so that your numbers can be compared with the expected ones.

Expected behaviour

Part 1: the largest Q-value at the start is 0.7738 and the greedy policy reaches G in every test episode, in six moves.

Part 2: the shortest safe path has six moves and the reward of 1 arrives with the sixth, so it is discounted five times: 0.955=0.77380.95^5 = 0.77380.955=0.7738.

Part 3: the Q-table stays at zero in the start state and the success rate is 0.

Part 4: in the reference run, α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 gives a success rate of 0.53 and α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05 gives 0.72. Across five seeds the first setting ranged from 0.15 to 0.73, and the second gave 0.72 each time. Solving the same MDP exactly by value iteration gives an optimal start value of 0.180 and a best possible success rate of 0.73 within 100 steps. Your figures will differ a little with another seed or Python version.

Hint 1

For part 2, count the moves on the shortest path that avoids the holes and remember that the reward arrives with the last move.

Hint 2

In part 3, work out what q[state].index(max(q[state])) returns when all four values are zero, and where that action takes the agent from the top-left corner.

Hint 3

In part 4 each target is one random sample of where the agent slipped. Consider what the update does with alpha = 0.5 when the targets for the same state-action pair alternate between 0 and a positive number.

Show solution
python
import random

MAP = ["SFFF", "FHFH", "FFFH", "HFFG"]
MOVES = [(0, -1), (1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0)]          # 0 left, 1 down, 2 right, 3 up
GAMMA = 0.95

def step(state, action, rng, slippery):
    if slippery:                                     # intended move or a perpendicular one, 1/3 each
        action = (action + rng.choice((-1, 0, 1))) % 4
    row, col = divmod(state, 4)
    d_row, d_col = MOVES[action]
    row, col = min(3, max(0, row + d_row)), min(3, max(0, col + d_col))
    cell = MAP[row][col]
    return row * 4 + col, float(cell == "G"), cell in "HG"

def train(slippery, episodes, alpha, seed=0, first_index_ties=False, constant_eps=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    q = [[0.0] * 4 for _ in range(16)]
    for episode in range(episodes):
        eps = constant_eps if constant_eps is not None else max(0.05, 1.0 - episode / (episodes / 2))
        state = 0
        for _ in range(100):                         # step limit: a truncation, not a termination
            best = max(q[state])
            if rng.random() < eps:
                action = rng.randrange(4)
            elif first_index_ties:
                action = q[state].index(best)
            else:
                action = rng.choice([a for a in range(4) if q[state][a] == best])
            nxt, reward, terminated = step(state, action, rng, slippery)
            target = reward if terminated else reward + GAMMA * max(q[nxt])
            q[state][action] += alpha * (target - q[state][action])
            state = nxt
            if terminated:
                break
    return q

def success_rate(q, slippery, episodes=2000, seed=123):
    rng, wins = random.Random(seed), 0.0
    for _ in range(episodes):
        state = 0
        for _ in range(100):
            state, reward, terminated = step(state, q[state].index(max(q[state])), rng, slippery)
            if terminated:
                wins += reward
                break
    return wins / episodes

def show(q):
    for row in range(4):
        cells = [MAP[row][c] if MAP[row][c] in "HG" else "<v>^"[q[row * 4 + c].index(max(q[row * 4 + c]))]
                 for c in range(4)]
        print("   " + " ".join(cells))

q = train(slippery=False, episodes=2000, alpha=0.5)
print(f"deterministic: max Q(start) = {max(q[0]):.4f}, success = {success_rate(q, False):.2f}")
show(q)
q = train(slippery=False, episodes=2000, alpha=0.5, first_index_ties=True, constant_eps=0.1)
print(f"first-index ties, constant epsilon 0.1: max Q(start) = {max(q[0]):.4f}, success = {success_rate(q, False):.2f}")
for alpha in (0.5, 0.05):
    q = train(slippery=True, episodes=20000, alpha=alpha)
    print(f"slippery, alpha {alpha}: max Q(start) = {max(q[0]):.3f}, success = {success_rate(q, True):.2f}")
text
deterministic: max Q(start) = 0.7738, success = 1.00
   v > v <
   v H v H
   > v v H
   H > > G
first-index ties, constant epsilon 0.1: max Q(start) = 0.0000, success = 0.00
slippery, alpha 0.5: max Q(start) = 0.122, success = 0.53
slippery, alpha 0.05: max Q(start) = 0.182, success = 0.72

Part 1 and 2. The arrows from S read down, down, right, down, right, right: six moves. Only the last one is rewarded, so the start value is 0.955=0.77380.95^5 = 0.77380.955=0.7738, and Q-learning reproduces it to four decimals because nothing in this environment is random. Arrows in cells the greedy path never visits are not meaningful.

Part 3. With every value at zero, index(max(...)) returns 0, which is "left". From the top-left corner that move changes nothing. At least nine steps in ten push against the wall, and whenever a random step moves it away, the greedy steps that follow are "left" again. Reaching G would need a run of several lucky exploratory moves, which does not happen in 2,000 episodes, and since no reward is ever seen no Q-value ever changes. Random tie-breaking, or an ε that starts at 1, removes the problem.

Part 4. On slippery ice the same state and action lead to different next states, so the target is a random variable and the Q-value should be its average. With α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 each update throws away half of what was learned and replaces it with the latest sample, so the estimates never settle and the greedy policy read from them is partly noise; that is why the success rate changes so much from seed to seed. With α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05 each estimate averages over roughly the last 20 samples, and the policy comes within a point of the best possible 0.73. Success cannot reach 1 here because some slips into holes are unavoidable whatever the agent intends.

Check your answer

  • Does the largest Q-value in the start state equal 0.7738 on the non-slippery lake, and does the greedy policy reach G in every test episode?
  • Does your target use the reward alone only when terminated is true, and not when the 100-step limit ended the episode?
  • With first-index tie-breaking and a constant epsilon of 0.1, are the start state's Q-values still zero after 2,000 episodes?
  • On the slippery lake with alpha = 0.05, is the greedy success rate close to 0.72, and does it stay there when you change the seed?
  • Can you say in one sentence why the best possible success rate on the slippery lake is below 1?

Exercise 2

REINFORCE on the corridor, and what a baseline buys

CodingAdvancedAbout 1 h (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

This exercise replaces the Q-table of the worked example with a policy and trains it with REINFORCE. The corridor is unchanged: cells 0 to 4, start in cell 1, entering cell 0 pays 1, entering cell 4 pays 10, both end the episode, and γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9.

The policy has two numbers (logits) for each of the cells 1, 2 and 3, and it moves right with probability

π(right∣s)=11+e θs,left−θs,right\pi(\text{right} \mid s) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{\,\theta_{s,\text{left}} - \theta_{s,\text{right}}}}π(right∣s)=1+eθs,left​−θs,right​1​

For this policy the derivative of log⁡π(a∣s)\log \pi(a \mid s)logπ(a∣s) with respect to the right logit is 1−π(right∣s)1 - \pi(\text{right} \mid s)1−π(right∣s) when the action was right and −π(right∣s)-\pi(\text{right} \mid s)−π(right∣s) when it was left. The derivative with respect to the left logit is the negative of that.

  1. All logits start at 0, so the policy is a coin flip in every cell. Compute the state values V(1)V(1)V(1), V(2)V(2)V(2) and V(3)V(3)V(3) of this random policy from its three Bellman equations.
  2. Keep the logits at 0 and play 20,000 episodes. For each episode compute the gradient estimate for the right logit of cell 1: the sum, over the visits to cell 1, of GtG_tGt​ times the derivative above. Compute it a second time with Gt−V(1)G_t - V(1)Gt​−V(1) in place of GtG_tGt​. Report the mean and the variance of both estimates.
  3. Now train. After each episode and for every step in it, add lr * weight * derivative to the right logit and subtract the same amount from the left logit. The weight is GtG_tGt​ for plain REINFORCE, or Gt−V(s)G_t - V(s)Gt​−V(s) with a learned critic updated by V[s] += 0.2 * (G - V[s]). Train for 300 episodes with lr = 0.3 for seeds 0 to 499, both ways, and count the runs that end with π(right∣1)\pi(\text{right} \mid 1)π(right∣1) above 0.9 and those that end below 0.1.

Requirements

  • Use the Python standard library only, and draw each action with a single call to random().
  • Compute the returns by walking backwards through the episode with G = reward + gamma * G.
  • In part 2 keep the logits fixed at zero; do not update the policy while measuring.
  • In part 3 update the critic for a step after its value has been used for the actor's update on that step.
  • Report the counts over the same 500 seeds for both variants.

Expected behaviour

Part 1: V(1)=2.372V(1) = 2.372V(1)=2.372, V(2)=4.160V(2) = 4.160V(2)=4.160 and V(3)=6.872V(3) = 6.872V(3)=6.872.

Part 2: both means are close to the exact gradient of 1.029 (the reference run gives 1.055 and 1.048). The variance is about 7.0 without the baseline and about 2.7 with it.

Part 3: in the reference run plain REINFORCE solves 460 of 500 runs and is stuck on the left in 40. With the learned baseline, 495 are solved and 5 are stuck. The critic of a solved run ends close to 8.1, 9.0 and 10.0 for cells 1, 2 and 3. Your counts will differ slightly if your random draws happen in a different order, but the gap between the two variants should remain.

Hint 1

For part 1, the equation for cell 1 is V(1) = 0.5 * 1 + 0.5 * 0.9 * V(2). Write the other two in the same way and substitute repeatedly until the numbers stop changing.

Hint 2

The exact gradient in part 2 is (expected number of visits to cell 1) * pi * (1 - pi) * (Q(1, right) - Q(1, left)) = 1.5 * 0.25 * (0.9 * V(2) - 1).

Hint 3

A run gets stuck when early left steps, each with a return of 1, are reinforced until the policy stops sampling right. Ask what sign the weight on a left step has once V(1) is larger than 1.

Show solution
python
import math, random, statistics

GAMMA = 0.9

def p_right(theta, state):
    """Softmax over two logits, written as a sigmoid of their difference."""
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(theta[state][0] - theta[state][1]))

def run_episode(theta, rng):
    state, steps = 1, []
    while state not in (0, 4):
        action = 1 if rng.random() < p_right(theta, state) else 0
        nxt = state + 1 if action else state - 1
        steps.append((state, action, {0: 1.0, 4: 10.0}.get(nxt, 0.0)))
        state = nxt
    return steps

# Part 1: state values under the uniform random policy, by repeated substitution.
v = {1: 0.0, 2: 0.0, 3: 0.0}
for _ in range(200):
    v = {1: 0.5 * 1 + 0.5 * GAMMA * v[2],
         2: 0.5 * GAMMA * v[1] + 0.5 * GAMMA * v[3],
         3: 0.5 * 10 + 0.5 * GAMMA * v[2]}
print("V under the random policy:", {s: round(x, 3) for s, x in v.items()})

# Part 2: mean and variance of the one-episode gradient estimate for the RIGHT logit of cell 1.
rng, theta = random.Random(0), {s: [0.0, 0.0] for s in (1, 2, 3)}
plain, with_baseline = [], []
for _ in range(20000):
    g, est_plain, est_base = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for state, action, reward in reversed(run_episode(theta, rng)):
        g = reward + GAMMA * g
        if state == 1:
            grad_log = 0.5 if action == 1 else -0.5          # (1 - p) or (-p) with p = 0.5
            est_plain += g * grad_log
            est_base += (g - v[1]) * grad_log
    plain.append(est_plain)
    with_baseline.append(est_base)
for name, xs in (("no baseline  ", plain), ("with baseline", with_baseline)):
    print(f"{name}: mean = {statistics.mean(xs):.3f}, variance = {statistics.pvariance(xs):.2f}")

# Part 3: training, with and without a learned baseline (the critic).
def train(use_baseline, episodes=300, lr=0.3, critic_lr=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    theta = {s: [0.0, 0.0] for s in (1, 2, 3)}               # actor
    value = {s: 0.0 for s in (1, 2, 3)}                      # critic
    for _ in range(episodes):
        g = 0.0
        for state, action, reward in reversed(run_episode(theta, rng)):
            g = reward + GAMMA * g
            weight = g - value[state] if use_baseline else g
            pr = p_right(theta, state)
            grad_right = (1.0 - pr) if action == 1 else -pr   # d log pi(action) / d theta_right
            theta[state][1] += lr * weight * grad_right
            theta[state][0] -= lr * weight * grad_right       # the left logit moves the opposite way
            if use_baseline:
                value[state] += critic_lr * (g - value[state])
    return theta, value

for use_baseline in (False, True):
    finals = [p_right(train(use_baseline, seed=seed)[0], 1) for seed in range(500)]
    label = "with baseline" if use_baseline else "no baseline  "
    print(f"{label}: solved (P(right) > 0.9) in {sum(p > 0.9 for p in finals)}/500 runs, "
          f"stuck on left (P(right) < 0.1) in {sum(p < 0.1 for p in finals)}/500")
theta, value = train(True, seed=0)
print("critic after training:", {s: round(x, 2) for s, x in value.items()})
text
V under the random policy: {1: 2.372, 2: 4.16, 3: 6.872}
no baseline  : mean = 1.055, variance = 6.97
with baseline: mean = 1.048, variance = 2.66
no baseline  : solved (P(right) > 0.9) in 460/500 runs, stuck on left (P(right) < 0.1) in 40/500
with baseline: solved (P(right) > 0.9) in 495/500 runs, stuck on left (P(right) < 0.1) in 5/500
critic after training: {1: 8.1, 2: 9.0, 3: 10.0}

Part 2. Both estimators have the same mean, because subtracting a number that depends only on the state does not change the expected gradient. Their variances differ by a factor of about 2.6. Without a baseline every return is positive, so every action taken is pushed up and the direction of learning comes only from some pushes being larger than others. With the baseline, a left step (return 1, expected 2.37) is pushed down and a right step that leads to the 10 is pushed up.

Part 3. The same effect decides whether training survives a large learning rate. In plain REINFORCE a few early left steps raise the left logit, the policy then samples left more often, and the habit feeds itself until right is almost never tried. Once the critic's value for cell 1 has risen above 1, the weight on a left step is negative, so the policy is pushed away from the small prize instead. The critic of a solved run converges on 8.1, 9.0 and 10.0, the values of always walking right, which are the Q∗(s,right)Q^*(s, \text{right})Q∗(s,right) entries from the worked example. This is an actor-critic method in its simplest form: a policy trained on advantages supplied by a learned value function.

Check your answer

  • Do your three state values satisfy all three Bellman equations when you substitute them back in?
  • Are the two mean gradient estimates within about 0.05 of 1.03 while the variances differ by more than a factor of two?
  • Does the baseline variant leave clearly fewer runs stuck on the left than plain REINFORCE at lr = 0.3?
  • After training with the baseline, is the critic close to 8.1, 9.0 and 10.0, and can you explain why those match the right-hand column of the worked example's table?

6Curated resources

Chosen for accuracy and usefulness, not search rank. Time figures are estimates.

  • Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (second edition, in progress) (opens in a new tab)

    Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto (draft hosted by Stanford University)

    BookIntermediateFreeAbout Several weeks; chapters 1 to 6 first (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The standard textbook treatment: bandits and exploration methods including ε-greedy and UCB, finite Markov decision processes and the Bellman equations, temporal-difference learning and Q-learning, and actor-critic methods. This copy is the authors' in-progress draft of the second edition, so chapter numbers differ from the finished book.
    When to use it
    When you want the derivations and the reasoning behind each update rule, or a definition you can rely on. Read chapters 2, 3 and 6 after this lesson.

  • Part 1: Key Concepts in RL — Spinning Up documentation (opens in a new tab)

    OpenAI

    CourseIntermediateFreeAbout 2 hours for parts 1 to 3 (estimate)

    What it teaches
    A compact mathematical introduction: trajectories, returns, the four value functions and their Bellman equations in part 1, a map of algorithm families in part 2, and a step-by-step derivation of the policy gradient, reward-to-go and baselines in part 3.
    When to use it
    When the formulas in this lesson went by too quickly, and before reading any policy-gradient paper.

  • Training an Agent - Gymnasium Documentation (opens in a new tab)

    Farama Foundation

    DocumentationBeginnerFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    A complete tabular Q-learning agent for Blackjack written against the standard Gymnasium environment interface, with an ε decay schedule, plots of training progress, a section on common training problems and a test of the trained agent with exploration switched off.
    When to use it
    Straight after the exercises here, to repeat tabular Q-learning with the library that nearly all RL code uses for environments.

  • Reinforcement Learning (DQN) Tutorial — PyTorch Tutorials (opens in a new tab)

    PyTorch

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 2 hours (estimate)

    What it teaches
    A full deep Q-network for CartPole in PyTorch: the replay memory, ε-greedy action selection with a decaying ε, the Huber loss on the TD error and soft updates of the target network, with the optimisation step explained piece by piece.
    When to use it
    When you are ready to move from a Q-table to a neural network and want working code to read and change.

  • Reinforcement Learning Tips and Tricks — Stable Baselines3 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    Stable-Baselines3 contributors

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 30 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Practical guidance from the maintainers of a widely used RL library: how RL differs from supervised learning in practice, why to run several seeds, how to evaluate an agent, which algorithm suits which action space, and how to design a custom environment and its reward.
    When to use it
    Before your first experiment with a library implementation, and again when a training run behaves strangely.
